question.worked_solution:
The laws of logarithms are:

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)+{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(ab)$ - the product rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)-{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(\frac{a}{b})$ - the quotient rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡({c}^{m})=m{log}_{n}⁡(c)$ - the power rule

Note that ${log}_{2}⁡(x{y}^{3})$ can be rewritten using the product and power rules as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(x{y}^{3}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(x)+{log}_{2}⁡({y}^{3}) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(x)+3{log}_{2}⁡(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${log}_{2}⁡(x)=k$ and ${log}_{2}⁡(y)=4,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(x)+3{log}_{2}⁡(y) & =k+3\cdot 4 \\  & =k+12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{log}_{2}⁡(x{y}^{3})=k+12.
$$
